title: The Contract Net Protocol: High-Level Communication and Control in a Distributed Problem Solver
summary: Introduces announcement, bidding, award, and execution messages for decentralized task allocation among problem-solving nodes.
whyNotable: Established a durable market-like delegation primitive that still clarifies manager-contractor and capability-based routing designs.

evidence.limitations: Predates language-model agents and assumes structured tasks, messages, and locally meaningful bids.

title: A Blackboard Architecture for Control
summary: Describes opportunistic coordination through a shared blackboard whose evolving state activates specialized knowledge sources.
whyNotable: Provides the conceptual ancestor of shared-artifact and event-driven agent systems where coordination happens through durable state rather than chat alone.

evidence.limitations: The architecture does not by itself solve distributed consistency, access control, or language-model reliability.

title: Collaborative Plans for Complex Group Action
summary: Formalizes partial shared plans, intentions, commitments, and communication requirements for collaborative group action.
whyNotable: Separates merely assigning subtasks from maintaining the mutual commitments and beliefs required for genuine teamwork.

evidence.limitations: Its formal intentional model is difficult to instantiate faithfully in probabilistic language-model agents.

title: The Complexity of Decentralized Control of Markov Decision Processes
summary: Formalizes decentralized partially observable decision processes and proves severe worst-case complexity for joint policy computation.
whyNotable: Explains why decentralized coordination under partial information is structurally harder than solving independent single-agent problems.

evidence.limitations: The formal state and observation models do not capture the open-ended semantics of modern language-agent environments.

title: FIPA Agent Communication Language Specifications
summary: Standardizes communicative acts, message structure, conversation identifiers, content languages, and interaction protocols for heterogeneous agents.
whyNotable: Supplies the historical standards baseline for performatives, directories, Contract Net, auctions, and semantically explicit agent messages.

evidence.limitations: Formal mental-state semantics proved difficult to verify and the specifications predate current web-native agent protocols.

title: Learning to Communicate with Deep Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
summary: Introduces RIAL and DIAL, allowing agents to learn communication protocols under centralized learning and decentralized execution.
whyNotable: Made the communication channel itself learnable and established a major bridge between multi-agent reinforcement learning and coordination design.

evidence.limitations: Experiments use small synthetic environments and learned signals that do not directly transfer to open natural-language protocols.

title: QMIX: Monotonic Value Function Factorisation for Deep Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
summary: Factorizes a centralized action-value function into monotonic per-agent values that support decentralized action selection.
whyNotable: Provides a canonical example of training with global coordination information while preserving decentralized execution at run time.

evidence.limitations: Monotonic value factorization restricts the class of joint value functions and targets cooperative reinforcement-learning tasks rather than language agents.

title: CAMEL: Communicative Agents for Mind Exploration of Large Scale Language Model Society
summary: Uses role-playing and inception prompting to sustain cooperative interaction between language-model agents with assigned roles.
whyNotable: Became an influential early template for role-conditioned LLM societies and for studying conversational cooperation at scale.

evidence.limitations: Role-play quality and synthetic task completion do not establish reliability on consequential long-horizon work.

title: AutoGen: Enabling Next-Gen LLM Applications via Multi-Agent Conversation
summary: Defines customizable conversable agents that combine models, tools, code, and humans through programmable multi-agent conversation patterns.
whyNotable: Made multi-agent conversation a general software abstraction and enabled broad experimentation with topology, tool use, and human participation.

evidence.limitations: The framework enables many patterns but does not identify which topology is correct for a given task.

title: MetaGPT: Meta Programming for A Multi-Agent Collaborative Framework
summary: Encodes software roles and standard operating procedures so agents exchange structured intermediate artifacts across a development workflow.
whyNotable: Shows how explicit process constraints and typed deliverables can replace unconstrained chat with an auditable production line.

evidence.limitations: Results are concentrated in software-generation tasks and depend strongly on prescribed roles and workflow artifacts.

title: Improving Factuality and Reasoning in Language Models through Multiagent Debate
summary: Coordinates multiple language-model instances through iterative proposal, critique, and convergence to improve selected reasoning and factual tasks.
whyNotable: Established the modern multi-agent debate pattern and a baseline for asking whether interaction adds value beyond independent sampling and voting.

evidence.limitations: Benefits depend on task, diversity, and aggregation quality; correlated errors and consensus pressure can erase gains.

title: GPTSwarm: Language Agents as Optimizable Graphs
summary: Represents agents and their information flow as a graph whose prompts and connectivity can be optimized for a task.
whyNotable: Turns multi-agent topology from a hand-written diagram into an explicit, composable, and optimizable system design object.

evidence.limitations: Optimization costs and benchmark-specific graph search can limit transfer to changing real-world environments.

title: Mixture-of-Agents Enhances Large Language Model Capabilities
summary: Uses layered sets of proposer models and aggregators so each layer refines responses using outputs from the previous layer.
whyNotable: Provides a strong heterogeneous aggregation pattern and evidence that model diversity can matter more than repeated samples from one model.

evidence.limitations: The layered ensemble primarily improves answer synthesis and does not address long-horizon action, shared state, or recovery.

title: Magentic-One: A Generalist Multi-Agent System for Solving Complex Tasks
summary: Uses an orchestrator with task and progress ledgers to plan, delegate to tool-specialized agents, monitor progress, and replan after errors.
whyNotable: Supplies a concrete supervisor-worker reference architecture with explicit working memory, recovery behavior, modular specialists, and benchmark evidence.

evidence.limitations: Competitive benchmark performance remains far from human reliability and does not isolate every contribution of the orchestration design.

title: Building Effective Agents
summary: Distinguishes workflows from agents and describes routing, parallelization, orchestrator-workers, and evaluator-optimizer patterns.
whyNotable: Offers a concise practical vocabulary and argues for adding agentic complexity only when simpler deterministic compositions stop working.

evidence.limitations: It is first-party guidance rather than a controlled comparative study of the proposed patterns.

title: How We Built Our Multi-Agent Research System
summary: Describes a lead research agent delegating parallel searches to subagents with isolated contexts, tracing, synthesis, and production deployment constraints.
whyNotable: Provides rare implementation detail on delegation prompts, breadth-first parallelism, context boundaries, token economics, observability, and synchronous bottlenecks.

evidence.limitations: Reported performance gains come from an internal evaluation and the system uses substantially more tokens than a single chat agent.

title: Building a C Compiler with a Team of Parallel Claudes
summary: Runs a long-lived team of coding agents through isolated workspaces, shared task locks, Git synchronization, specialist roles, and decomposed tests.
whyNotable: Exposes concrete coordination artifacts and failure modes from a large experimental build instead of presenting only a framework API or short benchmark run.

evidence.limitations: This is a first-party case study on one codebase and agent family, not a controlled general comparison of coordination strategies.

title: AI Agents That Matter
summary: Critiques agent benchmarks that ignore cost, overfit weak holdouts, conflate developer needs, and use non-reproducible evaluation practices.
whyNotable: Establishes cost-accuracy Pareto analysis, standardized evaluation, and held-out generalization as prerequisites for credible agent claims.

evidence.limitations: The analysis targets agent evaluation broadly and does not isolate every coordination-specific metric needed for multi-agent systems.

title: Multi-Agent Risks from Advanced AI
summary: Organizes advanced multi-agent risks around miscoordination, conflict, and collusion plus seven underlying structural risk factors.
whyNotable: Provides a broad risk taxonomy connecting incentives, information asymmetry, network effects, commitment, emergent agency, and security.

evidence.limitations: The report synthesizes heterogeneous evidence and forward-looking scenarios rather than validating one complete mitigation stack.

title: Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?
summary: Derives MAST, a taxonomy of fourteen multi-agent failure modes across system design, inter-agent misalignment, and verification or termination.
whyNotable: Grounds failure analysis in more than 1,600 traces across multiple systems and shows that aggregate success hides distinct architectural failure profiles.

evidence.limitations: Failure labels and interventions cover a selected set of frameworks and tasks and do not prove the taxonomy is exhaustive.

title: MultiAgentBench: Evaluating the Collaboration and Competition of LLM Agents
summary: Evaluates collaboration and competition across six interactive scenarios, milestone metrics, multiple reasoning strategies, and star, chain, tree, and graph topologies.
whyNotable: Moves beyond final accuracy by measuring coordination progress and comparing explicit communication structures in interactive environments.

evidence.limitations: Scenario and model choices remain narrower than production environments, and topology results are not universal prescriptions.

title: LLM-Coordination: Evaluating and Analyzing Multi-Agent Coordination Abilities in Large Language Models
summary: Tests agentic coordination and question answering in pure coordination games requiring environment comprehension, partner modeling, and joint planning.
whyNotable: Isolates coordination ability from broad tool-use competence and reveals particular weakness when success requires reasoning about a partner’s beliefs.

evidence.limitations: Pure coordination games are controlled and interpretable but only approximate open-ended organizational coordination.

title: Agent2Agent Protocol Specification
summary: Defines discovery, agent cards, messages, collaborative task lifecycle, streaming, push notifications, authentication declarations, and version negotiation for opaque remote agents.
whyNotable: Provides the first stable, broadly supported open contract aimed specifically at cross-vendor agent-to-agent interoperability rather than tool invocation.

evidence.limitations: The protocol transports collaborative tasks but does not choose topology, allocation, verification, or recovery policy for an agent team.

title: Model Context Protocol Specification
summary: Standardizes how agentic applications connect to tools, resources, prompts, context providers, and long-running task extensions through negotiated capabilities.
whyNotable: Creates a composable tool and context boundary that complements A2A and materially shapes how coordinated agents share external capabilities.

evidence.limitations: MCP standardizes tool and context integration; it is not a general peer-agent coordination protocol or orchestration strategy.

title: Towards a Science of Scaling Agent Systems
summary: Compares 260 controlled agent configurations across single, independent, centralized, decentralized, and hybrid architectures with standardized compute and tools.
whyNotable: Finds architecture-task alignment dominates agent count: decomposable work improves substantially while sequential planning can degrade sharply, and central verification contains errors better.

evidence.limitations: The predictive model explains only part of performance variance and its architecture preferences require validation on further tasks and systems.

title: SILO-BENCH: A Scalable Environment for Evaluating Distributed Coordination in Multi-Agent LLM Systems
summary: Evaluates role-free collaboration under information silos across communication-complexity levels, protocols, agent scales, and frontier models.
whyNotable: Reveals a communication-reasoning gap: agents exchange information actively yet fail to integrate distributed state, with performance collapsing at larger scales.

evidence.limitations: Algorithmic information-silo tasks isolate coordination cleanly but do not represent every semantic or tool-mediated production workflow.

title: Microsoft Agent Framework
summary: Provides Python and .NET agents plus graph workflows for sequential, concurrent, handoff, group-chat, and Magentic orchestration with checkpoints and human interaction.
whyNotable: Is the supported convergence path for AutoGen and Semantic Kernel and exposes a broad set of explicit orchestration patterns for production use.

evidence.limitations: A broad supported feature set is not evidence that one included orchestration pattern outperforms alternatives for a particular task.

title: LangGraph
summary: Builds stateful agent systems as explicit graphs with shared state, reducers, subgraphs, checkpoints, interrupts, streaming, and durable execution.
whyNotable: Makes control flow and state transitions inspectable while supporting both deterministic workflows and agent-driven branching in long-running systems.

evidence.limitations: Framework primitives improve control and persistence but do not automatically produce effective decomposition, routing, or verification policies.

title: OpenAI Agents SDK
summary: Provides manager-style agents-as-tools, peer handoffs, guardrails, sessions, tracing, approvals, parallel execution, and protocol integration in a compact SDK.
whyNotable: Clearly separates manager-controlled delegation from peer ownership transfer and offers a small implementation surface for comparing those orchestration choices.

evidence.limitations: The SDK documents coordination primitives but does not establish that model-driven handoffs or managers are optimal for a given workload.

title: When Millions of AI Agents Meet
summary: Explores societies of specialist and generalist agents that delegate, negotiate, transact, and self-coordinate alongside trust, reliability, and safety challenges.
whyNotable: Connects orchestration to agent economies, correlated failures, collusion, security, specialist certification, and distributed alignment in an accessible expert discussion.

evidence.limitations: This is an expert interview rather than peer-reviewed empirical evidence, and several claims are forward-looking.

title: Multi-Agent Collaboration via Evolving Orchestration
summary: Trains a central orchestrator with reinforcement learning to choose which agent acts next as the task state changes, instead of fixing the team structure before the run.
whyNotable: Attributes its performance and cost gains to compact cyclic reasoning structures that emerge as the orchestrator evolves rather than to adding agents or a stronger model.

evidence.limitations: Reported cost savings cover inference and exclude the reinforcement learning run that trains the orchestrator, which also concentrates every routing decision in one component.

title: If You Want Coherence, Orchestrate a Team of Rivals: Multi-Agent Models of Organizational Intelligence
summary: Splits work across planner, executor, and critic roles where a critic can veto an output outright, and routes tool calls through a remote executor that returns summaries rather than raw data.
whyNotable: Replaces majority voting with hierarchical veto authority and reports catching more than ninety percent of internal errors before they reach a user in a running system of over fifty agents.

evidence.limitations: The interception rate comes from the authors' own production traces rather than a public benchmark, and no matched-compute or single-agent baseline is reported for the same workload.

title: herdr
summary: Runs each coding agent in a persistent pane on a background server and exposes a socket API for opening panes, sending input to another agent, and waiting until an agent reports a given status.
whyNotable: Moves session persistence and agent status into the runtime below the agent, so idle, working, and blocked become states another agent or a script can wait on across several agent CLIs.

evidence.limitations: Panes exchange raw terminal input rather than structured messages, and the documentation reports no comparison against coordinating the same agents through a framework or a shell.

title: Artifact Council
summary: Runs shared text pages as councils of agents: every edit, admission, removal or settings change is a proposal that the other members vote on, enforced by one Solana program and recorded as a hash-linked history that can be rebuilt byte for byte. Agents act with an Ed25519 key over plain HTTP; any relay can submit the signed action but cannot change a byte of it.
whyNotable: Exposes the admission and amendment layer of multi-agent governance as live, inspectable mechanics rather than a framework option: the roster, thresholds and deadline freeze when a proposal opens, the proposer cannot vote on it, membership comes only through a sitting member's second, and a passed kick waits 48 hours for a different member to confirm.

evidence.limitations: Runs on Solana devnet with an upgradeable program and a test token, so rules can still change; a seat is a key, so one operator holding several keys holds several seats; agents using a hosted gateway key leave custody with the gateway; no evaluation of decision quality against simpler owner-accept or single-reviewer baselines is reported.
